subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Reading: Madhu Under the Banyan Tree

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (pp.88–92): teacher-led read-aloud with mid-story prediction pauses.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Madhu — a boy who loves food — and the magical banyan tree setting, drawing on the story title to invite curiosity about what a wish from a tree might mean.

Let us read (pp.88–92): teacher reads aloud expressively, pausing at p.89 to ask 'What do you think Madhu will do now?' and again at p.90 for 'What do you think will happen now?', gathering brief oral responses before continuing.

Teacher completes the read-aloud through the hiccup episode; students follow in their textbooks, noting unfamiliar food words (laddoos, matri, kachori, vada) which the teacher explains briefly in context.
Quick oral recap: teacher asks the class to name in order the three kinds of food Madhu received — sweets, fruits, savouries — reinforcing story sequence and food vocabulary before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The story carries a long chain of food names (laddoos, grapes, mangoes, matri, kachori, vada) that can blur into each other; pausing to let children echo each name aloud helps them stick. The two prediction pauses at pages 89 and 90 are the story's natural suspense points — hold them long enough for a few voices, then read on to confirm or surprise.
materials: Blackboard or chart listing food vocabulary: laddoo, matri, kachori, vada, kheer, sharbat, badam milk

periods.activity_title: Comprehension: Let Us Think — Answer and Discuss

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.93): four comprehension questions discussed and answered in class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites two or three students to retell what Madhu wished for and what happened next, refreshing the story in everyone's mind before moving to focused questions.

Let us think — A, questions 1 and 2 (p.93): teacher reads each aloud, students discuss in pairs for a moment, then share answers with the class; teacher guides the class to notice evidence for the old man's magical powers in the story.

Let us think — A, questions 3 and 4 (p.93): teacher poses questions 3 and 4 and encourages students to explain why the tree's gentle warning mattered and to list specific foods Madhu ate, building a shared response on the board.
Students write their own answers to all four questions in their exercise books, using the shared responses on the board as a guide; teacher circulates and reads a few aloud to close.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the full story read aloud together, students are now ready to revisit specific moments — the old man's arrival, the tree's warning, the food list — as evidence for their answers. Question 2 ('Do you think the old man had magical powers?') often yields lively disagreement; steer students back to the text to support their reasoning rather than settling it by assertion.

periods.activity_title: Think, Say and Listen: Hiccups, Water and Wishes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.93): four personal-experience speaking prompts on hiccups, water and wishes.
Let us listen — A (p.97): teacher reads two story excerpts; students listen and retell what happened next.

time_bands.activity: Let us think — B (p.93): teacher leads a guided conversation around the four prompts — hiccups, hiccup remedies, the importance of water, and what wish the student would make — taking responses from several students for each prompt and building a brief class consensus about water's value.

Teacher reads aloud the first transcript passage (p.97): 'Madhu said, Oh tree, let me have different types of food. Nothing else.' — reading it two to three times clearly, then pausing for students to tell the class what happened after that.

Teacher reads aloud the second transcript passage (p.97): 'As he was eating, he suddenly got hiccups. He wanted water.' — again two to three readings, then students share what happened next; teacher affirms correct story recall and gently corrects sequence errors.

Open discussion: teacher asks 'If you could make one wish for your whole class, what would it be and why?' — students speak in pairs first, then one pair shares with the class, modelling a complete spoken sentence to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task at p.97 asks students to recall what follows each excerpt — encourage them to use story language ('Then the tree said…', 'So Madhu asked for…') rather than single words. For the personal-wish question, children at this stage may give food-related answers echoing Madhu; invite them to think beyond food before moving on.
materials: Blackboard for brief vocabulary support if needed

periods.activity_title: Word Work: Food Sorting, Character Words and 'And' / 'But'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.94): sort story food items into Fruits, Sweets and Salty snacks baskets.
Let us learn — B & C (p.95): read character adjectives from the story; fill blanks with brave, polite, selfish, lazy.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn — D (pp.96–97): rewrite five sentence pairs using 'and' or 'but' as shown in class examples.

time_bands.activity: Let us learn — A (p.94): teacher draws three baskets on the board labelled Fruits, Sweets, Salty snacks and reads each Help Box word aloud; students call out the correct basket and teacher writes the word in it, then students copy the completed table.

Let us learn — B (p.95): teacher reads the three model sentences about Madhu, the old man, and the tree aloud, underlining kind, greedy, generous and asking what each tells us about the person; students then complete exercise C (p.95) by choosing from brave, polite, selfish, lazy for each character description.

Teacher introduces Let us learn — D (pp.96–97) by working through examples 1 and 2 together on the board — showing how 'and' joins similar actions and 'but' signals contrast — so students understand the rule clearly before practising the rest for homework.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often misplace jackfruit (it is a fruit) and kheer (it is a sweet, not a snack) — pausing on these two during the basket sort prevents the most common errors. When introducing the adjectives kind, greedy, generous, connect each word back to a specific moment in the story so children experience vocabulary in context rather than as isolated labels.
materials: Blackboard with three basket columns drawn

periods.activity_title: Word Work: Combining Sentences and Alliterative Pyramids

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — D (pp.96–97): rewrite five sentence pairs using 'and' or 'but' in class with teacher support.
Fun with Words — B & C (p.99): identify shared first letters in alliterative pyramids and write an original one using a chosen name.

time_bands.activity: Let us learn — D (pp.96–97): teacher takes up sentences 1–5 one by one, asking students whether the two ideas are similar (and) or contrasting (but) before a volunteer rewrites on the board; the class agrees on the final combined sentence and all record it.

Fun with Words — B (p.99): teacher writes 'Carrots / Cut Carrots / Chandu Cut Carrots' and 'Apples / Ate Apples / Anu Ate Apples' on the board; students identify the shared first letter in each pyramid and fill in the blanks together.

Fun with Words — C (p.99): students choose their own name or a friend's name, build their own alliterative pyramid in exercise books, then a few volunteers share their creations aloud to lively applause.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'and / but' task from the previous sitting is revisited here with full class support — students who attempted the homework will find this consolidating, while those who did not will complete the work now. For the alliterative pyramid, prompt children who are stuck by asking them to think of action words or food names that start with the same letter as their name.

periods.activity_title: Writing: Sentence Completion and Story Continuation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.100): discuss and complete four sentence starters about Madhu's actions and reasons.
Let us write — A (p.98): continue Vijaya's story from the given opening sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the four incomplete sentences from p.100 aloud and asks students to think quietly for a moment before discussing with a partner, so everyone has an idea to contribute.

Let us write — A (p.100): teacher takes each of the four sentence starters one by one — Madhu shared food because…, Madhu was happy because…, Madhu asked for savouries because…, Madhu asked for water because… — inviting responses and modelling how to write a complete, reason-giving sentence on the board; students write their own completed sentences.

Let us write — A (p.98): teacher reads the Vijaya story opening aloud ('Vijaya is a young girl… Each day…') and models one possible continuation sentence on the board, thinking aloud about daily village life; students then draft two or three sentences continuing the story independently.

Two or three volunteers read their Vijaya continuations aloud; class gives a quick thumbs-up for something they liked in each piece, and teacher points out one strong sentence per reading before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence-completion task about Madhu grounds the writing in familiar story events — encourage children to use because to explain reasoning rather than simply restating what happened. For the Vijaya continuation, some children may default to copying the style of Madhu's story; gently redirect them to imagine Vijaya's own life by asking 'What might a girl in a village do each morning?'

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text: Make a Fruit and Vegetable Table Mat

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (pp.100–101): make a table mat by drawing, tearing coloured paper and pasting to create a mosaic fruit design.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the step-by-step illustrations on pp.100–101 and reads all six steps aloud slowly, checking that students understand each action — draw, tear, stick — before distributing materials.
Students choose one or two fruits or vegetables to draw on their A4 sheet; teacher circulates to help with outlines, reminding them to draw large enough for tearing and pasting to fill the shape.

Let us do (pp.100–101): students tear coloured paper into small pieces and paste them inside their fruit outlines, choosing colours that match the fruit — red for apple, yellow for mango — filling the shape completely as a mosaic.

Students hold up their finished table mats and do a brief gallery walk, moving around the room to see classmates' designs; teacher invites two or three students to name the fruit they chose and one thing they learned about making the mat.
Teacher connects the mat to the story — all the fruits Madhu wished for are things we eat and need water to digest — closing with the theme that food and water together keep us healthy.

periods.teacher_notes: This craft connects directly to the fruits named in the story — bananas, mangoes, guavas, apples — so encourage children to pick a fruit Madhu actually received rather than any random shape. Tearing paper rather than cutting it is deliberate at this stage; if some children find the fine motor work difficult, allow them to make slightly larger pieces.
materials: Red, yellow, green, orange and purple coloured paper sheets

items.source_lo: Student predicts and infers story events using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Madhu's food wish, the magical banyan tree's warning, and the consequence of a hasty wish.
items.item_stem: The old man thanked Madhu and told him he could make a wish from the magical banyan tree. The tree gave Madhu a gentle warning to think carefully before wishing. Which of the following shows that Madhu did NOT think carefully before making his wish?

options.label: A
options.text: Madhu sat under the banyan tree every day at noon.

options.label: B
options.text: Madhu wished for different types of food forever without considering what else he might need.

options.label: C
options.text: Madhu shared his lunch with the old man who arrived.

options.label: D
options.text: Madhu asked the tree to stop giving him food.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this may not distinguish setting details from character decisions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a misreading — sharing food was the kind act, not the hasty wish.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student has confused the end of the story with the moment of wishing.

items.source_lo: Student predicts and infers story events using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Madhu's food wish, the magical banyan tree's warning, and the consequence of a hasty wish.
items.item_stem: Madhu got hiccups after eating all the food and desperately needed water, but the tree reminded him he had wished for food only — not water. What do you think Madhu learned from this experience? Give one or two reasons using details from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Madhu learned that water is more important than any amount of food. He had wished hastily without thinking, and his hiccups showed him that food alone is not enough to be well.

items.source_lo: Student retells story events and shares personal responses using guided conversation and listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Madhu's hiccups, the importance of water, personal wish-making, and story retelling from read-aloud excerpts.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read this sentence aloud: 'As Madhu was eating, he suddenly got hiccups. He wanted water.' Listen carefully. Then choose what happened next in the story.

options.text: Madhu looked around and found plenty of water near the food.
There was food everywhere but no water for Madhu.
The tree immediately gave Madhu a jug of water without question.
The tree told Madhu he had wished for food only, not water.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 2 is true: there was food everywhere but no water. Statement 4 is true: the tree reminded Madhu he had wished for food only, not water. Statements 1 and 3 are false.
